content: Suvorexant is unlikely to cause clinically significant inhibition of human cytochrome P450 enzymes, including CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, or CYP2D6. Additionally, no meaningful inhibition of transporters such as OATP1B1, BCRP, or OCT2 is anticipated. Chronic administration of suvorexant is not expected to induce the metabolism of drugs metabolized by major CYP isoforms. Specific in vivo effects on the pharmacokinetics of midazolam, warfarin, digoxin, and oral contraceptives are presented as changes relative to the interacting drug administered alone. In studies involving rasH2 mice, no evidence of suvorexant-induced neoplasms was observed at oral doses of 25, 50, 200, and 650 mg/kg/day. However, in a 2-year study in rats, increases in thyroid neoplasms (follicular cell adenoma and combined adenoma/carcinoma in high-dose females; follicular cell adenoma in midand high-dose males) and liver neoplasms (hepatocellular adenoma in high-dose males) were observed. These findings were consistent with increased TSH levels and hepatic enzyme induction, mechanisms believed to be specific to rodents. Plasma exposures (AUC) at doses not associated with drug-induced neoplasms in rats were approximately seven times higher than those in humans at the maximum recommended human dose (MRHD) of 20 mg. Suvorexant was negative in in vitro assays (bacterial reverse mutation and chromosomal aberration) and in vivo assays (mouse and rat micronucleus tests). In two separate studies, male and female rats treated with suvorexant prior to and during mating, and continuing in females to gestation day 7, showed increases in peri-implantation loss and resorptions, resulting in a decrease in live fetuses at the highest doses tested (1200 or 325 mg/kg). At the no-effect dose for adverse effects on fertility in males and females, plasma AUCs were approximately 20 times higher than those in humans at the MRHD. In dogs with hereditary narcolepsy, transient limb buckling and prone posture were observed when presented with food enrichment, a stimulus known to induce cataplexy. In a 2-year carcinogenicity study in rats, an increased incidence of retinal atrophy was observed at all doses. Plasma AUCs at the lowest dose tested were approximately seven times higher than those in humans at the MRHD. Subsequent studies in albino and pigmented rats showed delayed onset and lower incidence and severity of retinal atrophy in pigmented rats after approximately one year of dosing. Suvorexant was evaluated in three clinical trials in patients with insomnia characterized by difficulties with sleep onset and sleep maintenance. Two similarly designed, 3-month, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group studies (Study 1 and Study 2) included non-elderly (ages 18–64) and elderly (ages ≥65) patients randomized separately. In these studies, non-elderly adults (mean age 46 years; 465 females, 275 males) were treated with suvorexant 20 mg (n=291) or placebo (n=449). Elderly patients (mean age 71 years; 346 females, 174 males) were treated with suvorexant 15 mg (n=202) or placebo (n=318). In both studies, suvorexant 15 mg or 20 mg was superior to placebo for sleep latency, as assessed objectively by polysomnography and subjectively by patient-estimated sleep latency. Suvorexant was also superior to placebo for sleep maintenance, as assessed objectively by polysomnography and subjectively by patient-estimated total sleep time. The effects of suvorexant at night 1 (objective) and week 1 (subjective) were generally consistent with later time points. The efficacy of suvorexant was similar between women and men and, based on limited data, between Caucasians and non-Caucasians. Twenty-seven percent of patients treated with suvorexant 15 mg or 20 mg in Study 1 and Study 2 were non-Caucasians, with the majority (69%) being Asian. In a 1-month crossover study (Study 3), non-elderly adults (ages 18–64, mean age 44 years) were treated with placebo (n=249) and suvorexant at doses of 10 mg (n=62), 20 mg (n=61), or up to 80 mg. Suvorexant 10 mg and 20 mg were superior to placebo for sleep latency and sleep maintenance, as assessed objectively by polysomnography. Suvorexant was also evaluated at doses of 30 mg and 40 mg in the 3-month placebo-controlled trials (Study 1 and Study 2). The higher doses were found to have similar efficacy to lower doses but were associated with significantly more adverse reactions. In special safety studies, the effects of suvorexant on driving performance were evaluated in two randomized, double-blind, placeboand active-controlled, four-period crossover studies. These studies assessed next-morning driving performance 9 hours after nighttime administration of suvorexant in 24 healthy elderly subjects (≥65 years old, mean age 69 years; 14 men, 10 women) who received 15 mg and 30 mg suvorexant, and 28 non-elderly subjects (mean age 46 years; 13 men, 15 women) who received 20 mg and 40 mg suvorexant. Testing was conducted after one night and after eight consecutive nights of treatment. The primary outcome measure was the change in Standard Deviation of Lane Position (SDLP), a measure of driving performance, assessed using a symmetry analysis. The analysis showed clinically meaningful impaired driving performance in some subjects.
